CIA's Former Head of Science: In New Space Race, U.S. is Falling Behind- Glenn Gaffney #ufotwitter

Gaffney discuss space as an area of strategic, scientific, intelligence and military competition with Russia and China, and assess the United States' current positioning.

It was podcast interview episode of Intelligence Matters, host Michael Morell speaks with Glenn Gaffney, current Executive Vice President of strategic intelligence investor In-Q-Tel and former head of the CIA's Science and Technology Directorate.

Key details from interview 

It's based on an interview from the "Intelligence Matters" podcast with Glenn Gaffney, a 30-year CIA veteran who previously led the agency's Directorate of Science and Technology (the division focused on developing advanced tools and capabilities for intelligence work). At the time, he was Executive Vice President at In-Q-Tel (the CIA's nonprofit venture capital arm that invests in tech startups).

Gaffney warned that the U.S. had atrophied (weakened or declined) in key space capabilities—such as communications, observation/earth-imaging systems, and supporting infrastructure critical to intelligence and national security—after decades of reduced investment.

Root cause: Post-Cold War budget cuts following the fall of the Berlin Wall (late 1980s/early 1990s). The U.S. shifted priorities away from space spending, assuming a "peace dividend," while adversaries did not.

Consequences: He estimated it could take ~20 years to rebuild lost advantages. Capabilities once unique to the U.S. (e.g., seeing "over the Iron Curtain" via satellites) had eroded.

Competitors: Primarily China and Russia, which continued heavy investment in space tech, military applications, and related fields like biotech, machine learning, and AI (where China was amassing massive data to operationalize advances).

Positive note: He praised early moves toward creating the U.S. Space Force (announced by VP Pence in 2018 under the Trump administration) as a step to refocus and rebuild space capabilities, though it faced bureaucratic and congressional hurdles.

Broader warning: This is part of a larger "huge race" in emerging technologies. The U.S. must grapple with tough questions (e.g., balancing security needs with American values like privacy in AI/data use) and explain them to the public to stay competitive.

Note that the same words “emerging technologies” were used by both Luo Elizondo and Vladimir Putin.

While Putin and Gaffney did not clarify what this means, Luo Elizondo spoke about these capabilities and revealed more details.

In that letter to President Trump, he stated that they represent the most urgent and greatest threat to American global air security, which he called “Emerging-All Domains Technology.” 

Domains that include: Drones, UFOs and other advanced systems operating across the air, space, strike sea domains that are capable of surveillance reconnaissance and kinetic effects and only UFOs can exhibit all those effects simultaneously. 

Pretty wild statements from all sides and almost nobody noticed that.
